This isn't your imagination — and it isn't a temporary blip either. Multiple market signals point to a genuine structural shift in how UAE employers hire. Mercer's UAE forecast pegs salary increases at a modest 4% for 2026, reflecting a more cautious approach to locking in permanent headcount. Across the border, Cooper Fitch data shows Saudi salary growth of around 2% — a clear regional pattern of employers keeping fixed commitments tight. Meanwhile, recruitment giants like Robert Half and Hays are actively expanding their interim divisions, and recruiters on LinkedIn are openly predicting that contract hiring will rise as permanent hiring slows. The takeaway is simple: the UAE job market is moving toward a more flexible, agile hiring model — and smart job seekers should adjust their strategy accordingly.

Boards are accelerating AI adoption for enterprise decisions — procurement, risk assessment, workforce planning. The promise is faster, data-driven choices. But a pattern is emerging across boardrooms in 2026: boards delegate authority to systems they cannot audit, built on reasoning they cannot see, producing outcomes they cannot explain.

The governance gap is not whether the AI was accurate. It is who answers when it is wrong. A vendor contract awarded on opaque scoring. A hiring algorithm that winnows without a visible rule. Risk models that flag accounts for closure with no documented rationale. Each decision carries the board's authority, but the board did not make it, cannot retrace it, and in most cases cannot even ask the system how it reached its conclusion.

That gap is the definition of ungoverned delegation, and it is standard practice. When a decision cannot be traced back to its inputs, accountability becomes decorative. Accountability flows upward until it doesn't. AI is where the chain stops.

This is the layer collective intelligence exists to hold open. Not a cleaner algorithm, but a record where the reasoning survives contact with the decision. We opened the room on it today. When a board delegates to AI it cannot audit, who holds the AI accountable?

I negotiated my first $4,000/month remote contract through LinkedIn.
No job board.
No Upwork.
No “Are you hiring?” messages.
Just content → conversation → contract.

Here’s how it happened:
1. I posted consistently for some time.
Nothing viral.
Just specific Android engineering content around architecture, performance, and real production problems.
A UK fintech founder noticed my posts and reached out.

2. The first call wasn't about my rate.
I asked about their product, team, bottlenecks, and what they were struggling with.
I listened.
By the end, I understood the problem I could solve.

3. I sold the outcome, not my hours.
Instead of sending a CV, I sent a one-page proposal:
Their problem → My solution → Expected outcome → Rate

4. They pushed back on the price.
I didn't discount.
We talked about the cost of leaving the problem unsolved.

5. I offered a 2-week paid trial.
Same rate. Low commitment for them.
The trial turned into a 6-month contract.

The biggest lesson?

Content got me noticed.
The conversation built trust.
The proposal made the value clear.
The trial made saying yes easy.
That's the system.

The conversation around design in 2026 is shifting away from pixel-perfect mockups toward something far more structural: the interface as a machine-readable contract.

The most overlooked trend is the rise of Machine Experience Design, or MX. When an AI agent interacts with your product—to book a meeting, file a ticket, or update a record—it does not see the gradient or the animation. It reads the semantic HTML, the accessible labels, the data attributes behind each component. If your design system does not expose a structured schema alongside the visual layer, your interface becomes invisible to the agents your users are already delegating work to.

A non-obvious consequence of this shift is how it changes the design-to-development handoff. The next generation of design tools will need to export both a visual spec and a structured data contract that defines how an AI agent should interact with each element. This is not an accessibility overlay. It is a new design primitive. Teams that invest in this now will build products that are discoverable and usable by both humans and machines, which is the only path to scale in an agentic world.

Another change hiding in the 2026 trends is the move toward emotionally aware, reactive interfaces. The bold color palettes and adaptive layouts are not just aesthetic choices. They are reactive to context, user state, and even biometric feedback. But the real insight is not the technology. It is the ethical design challenge it creates. When your interface changes based on a user's emotional state, you are no longer a designer. You are a behavioral architect. The teams that will succeed are the ones that define clear boundaries for when and how this reactivity is triggered, and who audit for dark patterns before they ship.

For hiring managers evaluating senior design talent: the engineers and designers who understand MX and reactive context design are the ones who can build systems that work for both end-users and the AI agents acting on their behalf. They do not just make things look good. They design interfaces that are semantically rigorous, ethically grounded, and structurally discoverable. These are the people who will lead the next wave of product design.

How is your team preparing for the shift toward designing interfaces that must be readable by both humans and AI agents?

Web3 Teams Waste 6 Months Building the Wrong Product — Here's Why


Every Web3 team starts with a great idea. But most of them spend 6 months building something nobody wants. Here's why.


🔍 The Common Mistake:

- Start building before validating the idea

- Add features based on what's trendy

- Build in isolation

- Launch and realize nobody needs it

- Then pivot and waste another 6 months


🔍 What Actually Happens:


1. Premature Building

- The founder has an idea

- They start coding immediately

- No user research, no landing page, no waitlist

- They build for 6 months

- Then discover the market isn't there


2. Chasing Narratives

- AI is hot? Add AI features

- ZK is hot? Build on ZKK

- RWA is hot? Pivot to RWA

- The product becomes a patchwork of trends

- No coherent vision


3. No Distribution Plan

- They build the product first

- Think distribution comes later

- By launch time, they have zero audience

- Marketing becomes an afterthought

- Nobody knows they exist


4. Ignoring the Competition

- Assume they're building something unique

- Don't look at what's already out there

- Don't understand why competitors win or lose

- Build something that's slightly worse than what exists

- And nobody switches


5. Hiring Too Early

- Raise money

- Hire a team of 10 engineers

- Burn through capital fast

- Still haven't validated the product

- Run out of money


🔍 What Successful Teams Actually Do:


1. Validate Before Building

- Landing page first

- Waitlist, pre-sell, letters of intent

- Talk to 50 potential users

- Only build if there's real demand


2. Distribution First

- Build audience while building product

- Content, community, partnerships

- By launch time, people are waiting

- Don't build in a vacuum


3. Small Team, Fast Iteration

- 2-3 people building

- Release in weeks, not months

- Talk to users every week

- Pivot based on real feedback


The best Web3 teams aren't the ones with the most funding or the fanciest tech. They're the ones that validate early, distribute constantly, and iterate fast.


We've seen this pattern a hundred times. The teams that win aren't the ones that build the most. They're the ones that build what people actually want.

What an outstanding afternoon at ChamberSOUTH’s Perspectives from the Bench: Leadership, Law & Community Luncheon. Proud to be there representing Esquire Deposition Solutions, LLC and learning from an exceptional panel of Judges Bronwyn Miller, Migna Sanchez-Llorens, Jorge A. Pérez Santiago, and Luis Perez-Medina, expertly moderated by Jose M. Ferrer from Mark Ferrer & Hayden.

I’ve attended and moderated A LOT of legal programs over the years, and this one delivered practical takeaways for lawyers and business leaders alike:

* AI is an incredible tool, but verify everything. Efficiency does not replace judgment, accuracy, or professional responsibility.

* Preserve the record. What happens at the trial level can determine what happens on appeal. When the record matters, make sure you have a court reporter. At Esquire, we have more than 1,000 incredible court reporters nationwide, and preserving the record is at the core of what we do. So yes, I know a few good ones.

* Florida’s new civil procedure rules have changed the pace of litigation. Prepare early, preserve documents, understand your discovery obligations, and do not assume a continuance will cure a lack of preparation.

*For business owners, preparation starts long before litigation. Clear contracts, strong recordkeeping, document preservation, and experienced counsel matter.

One of the business owners in the room also asked a great and very practical question: How do you find the right lawyer?

During my time as Vice Chair of The Florida Bar’s Citizens Advisory Committee, under the leadership of The Florida Bar President elect Paige Greenlee, we worked on consumer resources and pamphlets addressing exactly that, including when to seek legal counsel, how to find a lawyer, what questions to ask, and what to consider before hiring one. I’ll share that Florida Bar resource in the comments for anyone who may find it helpful.

A huge congratulations to my dear friend Michelle Pelaez , Adriana Verdeja , Rick Alberty , and the entire ChamberSOUTH team. 
Substantive, timely, practical, and exactly the kind of conversation our legal and business communities need. And personally, I was in legal nerd heaven. 

Proud to have Esquire Deposition Solutions, LLC  in the room supporting these conversations and the legal professionals who move our profession forward.

A few WCS-related job opportunities have landed in my inbox lately, so here’s a demo of one of my earlier side projects. 🎬

I built this WCS (Warehouse Control System) project while learning React, drawing on my previous warehouse automation experience.

I planned the features and architecture myself, building and testing one function at a time before putting everything together.

Basically, LEGO with warehouse logic. 🧱😂

That’s also how we tested at customer sites: verify individual functions first, then work through complete scenarios.

My newer projects take a different approach: I give an AI agent the overall structure and requirements, then let it handle the implementation details.

The difference? My WCS was designed with server and hardware integration in mind from day one, so connecting it could require relatively small changes.

An agent needs those requirements upfront too. Otherwise, connecting real hardware later could mean major changes to the architecture and features.

More time. More tokens. More “wait… we need to rebuild THAT too?” 😂

Combining both approaches sounds like the sweet spot to me: bring the engineering experience, then let the agent help build. 😎

I’m happy to chat about the project, but anything confidential from my previous employer stays confidential. 🤐

—

Now for a little job-search rambling… ☕

Based on my experience, some of these job descriptions give me this vibe:

“Urgent: manager needed to put out fires. Six-month contract.” 🚒😂
Canada may have plenty of applicants, but finding the right person early still matters.

Having handled customer projects independently, I can’t help wondering: if hiring takes two months, how much time is left for the new hire to learn the software and hardware before jumping into the fire?

On our projects, we had people preparing before development even started.

A former manager once told me:
“How smoothly on-site testing goes depends on how much you prepare before you get there—how well you know your code and architecture, and whether you’ve thought through where to start debugging when things go wrong.”

This isn’t just a “show up and tighten a few screws” kind of role. Understanding the whole system takes time—even when the job description says “urgent.”

Of course, with unlimited time for on-site testing… pretend I never said anything. XDD 😂

AI may help applicants get through the door, but the interview still needs to reveal what is real.

In nonprofits, we cannot afford to hire only from polished language. The interview has to help us see past the AI fluff and understand the candidate’s actual applied skills.

That means asking questions tied to the real work:

“I noticed your resume mentions program oversight. Can you walk me through what you were responsible for day to day?”

“You listed experience with grant or contract reporting. What information did you track, who reviewed it, and what happened when something was missing?”

“You mentioned working across departments. Tell me about a time program, finance, and operations needed different things from you at the same time. How did you manage that?”

This is also part of giving applicants a realistic job preview. They should leave the interview with a clear picture of the role, the pace, the expectations, and the judgment the position requires.

Hiring should not just sound good on paper. It needs to hold up in real nonprofit life.

Attrition & Freezes: The CEO previously detailed plans to freeze hiring for traditional roles through 2027, choosing not to backfill standard vacancies and letting AI absorb the workload.

I've seen a lot of grumbling about the "new hiring process". I feel this acutely. I'm 57, and I have a felony. Don't be judgey I served my sentence, but that doesn't seem to be enough.

I have to contend with phone interviews conducted by people who aren't doing the hiring, and don't actually know the required skills of the job in question. They are attempting to compile a Meyers-Briggs personality profile before even identifying if I'm a qualified candidate.

Think I'm joking? Take half an hour and apply for a job at Walmart, or Taco Bell. Two places of employment for which I am extremely over qualified, but almost immediately discounted because I have a felony.

I have years of experience supporting Quickbooks, and recently completed a phone interview to work for a company that supports Quickbooks. The phone interview went extremely well, to the point the interviewer wanted to put me in a higher paying position because of my experience. However, my background check reported my felony, which I voluntarily reported to them, and now I've been ghosted.

I'm submitting resumes by the dozens, which seem to only lead me down another survey or personality-hole and wastes my time, while clogging my inbox with A.I. generated responses of thanks but no thanks.

I don't want to work remotely, and I'm not interested in contract work. I'm beginning to feel that my only recourse is to once again start my own business.
